sections.html:
Evansville is the Vanderburgh County seat, on a bend of the Ohio River in southwestern Indiana. It is the third-largest city in the state, with 117,298 people at the 2020 census and an estimate of 116,176 as of July 2025. The city covers about 47.9 square miles.

Owners hold a slim majority of housing at 54.6%. Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $143,100, owners with a mortgage pay a median $1,150 a month, and median gross rent is $975. The city has 53,095 households averaging 2.12 people.

Thirteen neighborhoods are listed as National Register historic districts, and Riverside is known for tree-lined brick streets and turn-of-the-century homes. Indiana's seller disclosure form asks whether a property sits in a locally designated historic district, so owners in those areas should have an answer ready.

sections.h2: Flood risk and the levee system
sections.html:
Evansville sits behind a levee system built after the 1937 Ohio River flood. The river crested at 53.7 feet on January 31, 1937, the flood covered about 500 city blocks, and the city was placed under martial law.

The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers began construction in 1939 and finished in 1994. The system includes 17 miles of earth levees and concrete floodwalls plus 19 pumping stations, and it protects against flood water up to 57 feet. The Evansville-Vanderburgh Levee Authority District maintains it.

  • The eastern levees closely follow I-69.
  • Pigeon Creek has been widened and leveed, and Ohio River backwater affects the whole county.
  • The creek's average annual peak flow at the Fort Branch gauge rose from about 2,350 to 2,820 cubic feet per second over 35 years.

Indiana's seller disclosure asks whether you know the property is in a FEMA flood plain. A buyer or lender may also want flood zone and insurance details, so find out your parcel's status before you sell. Humid summers and about 45 inches of rain a year make roof condition, drainage and basement moisture standard inspection topics too.

sections.h2: Older homes and the local economy
sections.html:
Downtown grew from an original plat of about 200 acres and still holds early twentieth-century buildings. Hardwood furniture made Evansville a manufacturing center, with 41 factories by 1900, and many of the older houses around town date from that era. Homes of that age often have original roofs, wiring and plumbing that buyers want priced in.

Today health care, manufacturing and finance employ many residents. Deaconess Health System and Ascension St. Vincent are major health care names, Berry Global and OneMain Financial are headquartered here, and two universities, the University of Evansville and the University of Southern Indiana, bring students and staff. Job changes at employers like these are one reason homes come up for sale on short notice.

Evansville regulates rental dwellings under Chapter 15.16 of its municipal code, and the Building Commission runs a rental registry. Registration is required for substandard rental buildings and voluntary for well-kept ones. The city has moved registrations to an online platform.

Registration typeFee per dwelling unitWhat it involves
Required$100.00Substandard rental buildings
Voluntary$10.00Signed affidavit that the building meets the property maintenance code

A voluntary permit lasts one year or until title transfers, and covers up to $3,000 of maintenance work per unit.

Owners must report an ownership change within 30 days, and a prior registration expires 30 days after title transfers, so the new owner registers again. Code officials may give an owner at least 10 calendar days to fix a violation, and an owner ordered to register may appeal in writing within 10 calendar days of service. Questions go to the Rental Registry at the Building Commission, 812-436-7887.

sections.h2: Permits, property tax and code enforcement offices
sections.html:
City and county offices share the Civic Center Complex at 1 NW Martin Luther King Jr. Blvd., Evansville, IN 47708. The Building Commission is in Room 310, the Department of Metropolitan Development in Room 306, and the Area Plan Commission, which handles zoning and improvement location permits, in Room 312.

  • Building Commission, permits and inspections: (812) 436-7885.
  • Vanderburgh County Auditor: Room 208, (812) 435-5369.
  • Vanderburgh County Treasurer: Room 210, (812) 435-5248.

Property maintenance enforcement, including weeds, trash and existing structures, falls under the Building Commission. If you have an open violation, tell the title company early so the closing plan accounts for it.

Indiana property tax is due in two installments, in May and November. A payment up to 30 days late carries a 5% penalty, and one later than that carries 10%. Payments go to the Vanderburgh County Treasurer. When you sell, the closing agent normally settles the tax with you and the buyer, so ask for a figure before the settlement date.

sections.h2: Selling with a mortgage or taxes owed
sections.html:
Evansville sellers should also confirm where their offices are before closing day. The Auditor is in Room 208 and the Treasurer in Room 210 of the Civic Center Complex, and both can answer questions about your parcel. The Building Commission, in Room 310, can tell you whether an inspection or permit is open on the house.

Most sellers have some balance to clear. Ask your lender for a payoff letter and the Treasurer for the current tax figure. Both come out of your proceeds at closing, and you receive the rest. With a cash sale you decide how fast this happens, and no buyer's lender has to approve the house before the money is released.

sections.h2: Which Evansville owners sell for cash?
sections.html:
A home here can come with a long list of repairs: an older roof, damp basement, outdated systems or a house in a flood-prone spot. Others are rentals that have drawn a code notice, or inherited houses where the family lives elsewhere. Selling as-is means you do not have to repair, stage or show the house to many people.

  1. Call with the address and a few notes about condition.
  2. We view the house and send a written cash offer.
  3. A title company handles the search and paperwork.
  4. You pick the closing date, and the proceeds pay off any lien or tax balance first.

If the house is a rental, bring the registration paperwork and any code notices. If an estate owns it, bring the court paperwork and the names of every heir. If the house sits near Pigeon Creek or the river, tell us what you know about past water. Honest answers up front keep the closing on schedule.

The offer will usually sit below a fully renovated retail sale. Compare it with what a listing would net after repairs, commission and months of carrying costs, and ask for the terms in writing.

faqs.q: Is Evansville in a flood zone?
faqs.a: Parts of the city are protected by a levee system of 17 miles of levees and floodwalls and 19 pumping stations. Your own parcel's FEMA status depends on its location, so check before listing, because Indiana's disclosure form asks about it.

faqs.q: Do Evansville landlords have to register their rental properties?
faqs.a: Substandard rentals must register at $100.00 per unit, while well-maintained rentals may register voluntarily at $10.00 per unit. Call the Rental Registry at 812-436-7887 to confirm which applies.

faqs.q: When are Evansville property taxes due?
faqs.a: In May and November. Late payments carry a 5% penalty up to 30 days and 10% beyond that.

faqs.q: What is the median home value in Evansville?
faqs.a: The median for owner-occupied units is $143,100. Your own house may differ based on condition and neighborhood.

faqs.q: What happens to a rental registration when I sell in Evansville?
faqs.a: Ownership changes must be reported within 30 days, and a prior registration expires 30 days after title transfers. The new owner registers again.
